passages.t: Zacchaeus, up a tree, and the Son of Man who seeks the lost
passages.happening:
Jesus enters Jericho and is passing through. A man named Zacchaeus lives there, “a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy” (verse 2). He wants to see who Jesus is, but he is short and the crowd is in the way. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree beside the road.

When Jesus reaches the spot, he looks up and calls him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today” (verse 5). Zacchaeus hurries down and welcomes him with joy. Everyone who sees it starts to grumble: “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (verse 7).

Zacchaeus stands and speaks to the Lord: “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold” (verse 8). Jesus answers, “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story. It is the last meeting on Jesus' long road to Jerusalem, which began at 9:51. Jericho was the last town before the steep climb up to the city.

Tax collectors in this region mostly collected tolls and customs on goods moving along the roads. The right to collect was sold to contractors, who paid in advance and then made their living from what they collected. Many Jews hated these men as cheats who worked for foreign rulers (see the note on 3:10-14). Zacchaeus is a ‘chief’ tax collector. The Greek word, architelōnēs, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He probably held the contract for the district and had other collectors working under him. That would explain both his money and his name in the town.

The tree was a sycamore-fig, a kind of wild fig common in the hot Jordan valley. It has a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb. Many readers think a rich man of his rank would have looked foolish running ahead and climbing a tree in front of the town. Zacchaeus does not care. He wants to see.

But the story turns. Zacchaeus came to see Jesus, and Jesus sees him first. He calls him by name, and says he ‘must’ stay with him. In Luke ‘must’ is the word for God's plan (see the book page's key words). ‘Today’ is Luke's word for the moment God's promise arrives (2:11; 4:21; 23:43). To eat in a man's house was to accept him, which is why the crowd grumbles, as the Pharisees and scribes had grumbled before: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (15:2).

The chapter before told of a rich ruler who went away sad, “because he was extremely wealthy” (18:23), and the disciples asked who could be saved. Jesus answered, “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (18:27). Here is a very wealthy man who is saved. The camel goes through the eye of the needle.

The word Zacchaeus uses for ‘cheated’ means to squeeze money out of people by threats or false charges. The only other place it appears in the New Testament is where John the Baptist tells soldiers not to do it (3:14). Zacchaeus does not pretend he is clean.

‘A son of Abraham’ means a member of the family God promised to bless through Abraham. The town had written Zacchaeus off. Jesus writes him back in. Luke has already told of ‘a daughter of Abraham’ whom Jesus set free (13:16).
passages.ot:
Zacchaeus measures his promise against the Law, and goes beyond it. The Law said that a person who cheated someone “must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner” (Leviticus 6:5). Four times over was the penalty for a stolen sheep that had been killed or sold: “four sheep for a sheep” (Exodus 22:1). When Nathan told King David about the rich man who took a poor man's lamb, David said the man “must pay for the lamb four times over” (2 Samuel 12:6). Zacchaeus treats himself as that kind of thief, and gives half of everything to the poor on top.

‘To seek and to save the lost’ echoes the prophet Ezekiel. The shepherds of Israel had failed, and God said he would look after his flock himself: “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). Jesus takes up the work God said he would do.
passages.hard:
Did Zacchaeus say ‘I give’ or ‘I will give’? In Greek both of his verbs are in the present tense: ‘I give’ and ‘I give back’. Readers take this in two ways.

Most read it as an announcement. The present tense can speak of something about to begin, so Zacchaeus is saying, ‘From now on, I give half, and I will repay.’ On this reading the story is a conversion. Jesus' welcome comes first, and Zacchaeus' life turns in response. Many English Bibles translate it that way, as the Berean Standard Bible does with ‘I will repay’.

Some read it as a description of his habit. Zacchaeus is defending himself against the crowd: ‘I already give half to the poor, and whenever I find I have cheated someone, I repay it four times over.’ On this reading Jesus is not converting a villain but standing up for a man whom the town had judged wrongly, and saying he belongs to Abraham's family after all.

The Greek allows both, and careful scholars hold each. These notes do not choose. Either way, two things are clear. Jesus came to Zacchaeus before Zacchaeus said a word about money, so the giving is not the price of the welcome. And salvation in Luke reaches a person's money. A faith that never touches the purse is not the faith Luke describes.
passages.asks: Jesus stopped under the tree that everyone else walked past, and he called the man by name. Ask whom you have already decided is beyond God's reach, and whether you would grumble if Jesus went to their house. If you carry shame about money, about debts you caused or people you cheated, notice the order here. The welcome comes first. Then the repair follows, and it is real: it reaches the people who were wronged. Ask what that repair might look like for you.

passages.t: The ten minas, and the king who went away
passages.happening:
The people are listening. Jesus is near Jerusalem, and they think the kingdom of God is about to appear at once. So he tells a parable (verse 11).

A man of noble birth goes to a distant country to be made king, and then to return. Before he leaves, he gives ten of his servants a mina each and says, ‘Conduct business with this until I return’ (verse 13). But his subjects hate him, and send a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us’ (verse 14).

He comes back as king and calls his servants. The first has turned one mina into ten, and is given ten cities to rule. The second has made five, and is given five cities. A third brings back the mina wrapped in a cloth: ‘I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man’ (verse 21). The king answers, “I will judge you by your own words” (verse 22). If he thought that, why did he not at least put the money in the bank to earn interest? The mina is taken from him and given to the one who has ten. ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him’ (verse 26).

The parable ends with the king's order about the subjects who did not want him: “bring them here and slay them in front of me” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
A mina was a sum of silver worth a hundred drachmas. A drachma was about a day's wage, so a mina was something like a hundred days' pay, about three or four months of work. That is real money, but not a fortune.

Matthew tells a similar parable, the talents (Matthew 25:14-30). A talent was worth sixty minas, about twenty years of a worker's wages, and Matthew's servants are given different amounts. In Luke every servant gets the same small sum. What sets them apart is only what they did with it. The reward fits Luke's line, “Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much” (16:10). And the reward is not rest. It is more work: cities to govern.

Luke's version also has a second story woven in, found only here: a nobleman who goes abroad to be made king, citizens who send a delegation saying they do not want him, and his return. Jesus' hearers knew a story very like it. When Herod the Great died, around 4 BC, his son Archelaus sailed to Rome to have the Emperor Augustus confirm him as ruler. The Jewish historian Josephus tells that a delegation of fifty Jews went too, and more than eight thousand Jews living in Rome joined them, to ask Augustus not to put a Herod over them at all. Augustus gave Archelaus part of his father's kingdom, though not the title of king. He ruled so harshly that in AD 6 Augustus removed him and sent him into exile. Archelaus had a palace at Jericho, where Jesus has just been. Many readers think Jesus' hearers would have caught the echo. Luke does not say so, and the parable is not about Archelaus. It borrows the shape of a story everyone knew.

Some scholars think Luke, or the source he used, joined two parables into one. Others think Jesus told it this way himself. Either way, it speaks to two groups at once: servants who must be faithful while the king is away, and a city about to say, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us.’

The point is aimed at the hope in verse 11. The crowd expects the kingdom to appear at once. The parable says the king must first go away to receive it, there will be a time of work while he is gone, and then he will return. Luke's readers knew where Jesus went: to the cross, the resurrection, and heaven, with the promise that he “will come back in the same way” (Acts 1:11).
passages.ot:
The Old Testament says that everything a person has belongs to God first: “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). The servants own nothing. They look after what is their master's.

The picture of a king who goes to receive his kingdom recalls Daniel's vision of “One like the Son of Man” who came to the Ancient of Days and was given “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:13-14). Jesus calls himself the Son of Man.
passages.hard:
Is the harsh king a picture of Jesus? The third servant calls him harsh, and the king answers, “I will judge you by your own words”. Most readers think the king is not agreeing that he is harsh. He is judging the servant by the servant's own picture of him (see the note on Matthew 25:14-30). The first two servants did not find their master hard. Fear made the third one hide what he was given. Parables often use rough human figures to make a point by contrast, as with the unjust judge (18:1-8). A few modern readers turn the story around and read the king as a greedy ruler and the third servant as an honest man who refused to join in. Most think that goes against the way Luke frames it. It does remind readers how a story about money sounds to the poor.

Verse 27 must be said plainly. It is a line inside a parable, spoken by a character in a story. It is never a warrant for violence, and no one may use it to harm anyone. Readers explain its place in the story in more than one way. Some read it as the end that comes to those who refuse God's king, the final judgment that the New Testament gives to Christ, who is “appointed by God to judge the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42). Many link it to what comes a few verses later, when Jesus weeps over the city that will not have him and foresees its ruin (19:41-44). Either way, the king in Luke who speaks this parable is the same one who rebuked his disciples when they wanted to call down fire on a village that refused him (9:54-55), who healed the ear of a man who came to arrest him (22:51), and who prayed for those who crucified him (23:34).
passages.asks: Each servant got the same small sum. The question was never how much they had, but whether they used it for the master while he was away. Ask what Jesus has put in your hands: time, money, a skill, a word you could say. And ask what picture of God you carry. The servant who failed was the one who was afraid. If you think of God as hard and grasping, you may hide what he has given you to keep from getting it wrong.

passages.t: The King comes down the Mount of Olives, and the stones
passages.happening:
Jesus goes on ahead, up to Jerusalem. Near Bethphage and Bethany, on the Mount of Olives, he sends two disciples to bring a colt that no one has ever ridden. If anyone asks why, they are to say, ‘The Lord needs it.’ It happens just as he said. They throw their cloaks on the colt and put Jesus on it, and people spread their cloaks on the road (verses 28-36).

As he comes to the way down from the Mount of Olives, “the whole multitude of disciples began to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen” (verse 37): “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” (verse 38).

Some Pharisees in the crowd say, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” He answers, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out” (verses 39-40).
passages.hearers:
Mark, Matthew and John all tell of this entry, and the notes on Mark 11:1-11 explain the colt, the cloaks spread like a welcome for a king (2 Kings 9:13), and the crowds at Passover. Luke tells it his own way.

Luke has no palm branches and no ‘Hosanna’, the Hebrew cry. His readers were mostly Greek speakers. He gives the words of Psalm 118 and adds one word, ‘King’, as John does too. There is no mistaking what the disciples are saying.

Luke's praise comes from ‘the whole multitude of disciples’, praising God for the miracles they had seen. The cry ‘Peace in heaven and glory in the highest’ takes the reader back to the night Jesus was born, when the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (2:14). Now the peace is ‘in heaven’. Many readers think Luke means that the city is about to refuse the peace offered on earth, as the next verses say.

Luke places the shout at the way down from the Mount of Olives. Coming over that ridge from the east, a traveller sees the whole city across the valley, with the temple facing him. It is from there that Jesus will see the city and weep (verse 41).

Only Luke tells of the Pharisees' request and Jesus' answer about the stones. The Pharisees may have feared what the Romans would do if a crowd hailed a king at Passover. Not all Pharisees were against Jesus; some had warned him about Herod (13:31). But Jesus will not silence the praise. If people say nothing, creation itself would speak.
passages.ot:
The disciples' words come from Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.” Pilgrims sang this psalm at the great feasts.

Luke does not quote it, but the prophet had said, “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt” (Zechariah 9:9). Matthew and John quote that verse here. Some readers also remember that when David made Solomon king, he said, “Set my son Solomon on my own mule” (1 Kings 1:33). The son of David rides to his city.

The stones that cry out echo the prophet Habakkuk, who warned a man who built his house by cheating: “For the stones will cry out from the wall” (Habakkuk 2:11).
passages.hard:
Did the same crowd that cheered on Sunday shout ‘Crucify him’ on Friday? Sermons often say so. Luke does not. He says the praise came from ‘the whole multitude of disciples’, the people who had followed Jesus and seen his miracles. The crowd before Pilate (23:18-23) is not said to be the same people. It is wise not to say more than the Gospel says.

What does Jesus mean about the stones? Some take it as a way of saying that the truth about him cannot be kept quiet: if his followers were silenced, creation would speak. Others hear the warning in Habakkuk, where stones cry out against wrong, and connect it to the stones of the city that will be torn down (verse 44). The two readings can sit together.
passages.asks: The Pharisees wanted the praise kept down, to keep things calm. Ask whether you ever keep your own thanks to God quiet because it might cause a stir. And ask what kind of king you are welcoming. This one comes on a borrowed colt, and he is about to weep.

passages.happening:
As Jesus comes near and sees the city, “He wept over it” (verse 41). He says, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes” (verse 42).

Then he speaks of what is coming: “For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side” (verse 43). “They will level you to the ground”, the city and “the children within your walls”. “They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this. The word for ‘wept’ means to weep aloud, the crying of mourners. When Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, John uses a quieter word (John 11:35). Here the King, in the middle of the shouting, breaks down.

This is the second time in Luke that Jesus grieves over the city. Earlier, before he reached it, he said, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!” (13:34). A hen is not a strong animal. When danger comes, she spreads her wings and puts her own body between her chicks and the threat.

‘The time of your visitation’ uses a word Luke chose with care. At the start of the book Zechariah sang that God “has visited and redeemed His people” (1:68), using a verb from the same family. In the Old Testament God ‘visits’ his people to rescue them, or to judge them. Jesus' coming was God's visit. The city did not see it.

About forty years later the city fell. The Jewish revolt against Rome began in AD 66. In AD 70 a Roman army under Titus took Jerusalem, and the temple burned. Josephus, who was there, says the Romans built a wall right round the city so that no one could get in or out, and finished it in three days. Famine followed, then the city was stormed.

On the Mount of Olives today there is a small church called Dominus Flevit, Latin for ‘the Lord wept’. It was built in the 1950s, in the shape of a tear, with a window that looks across the valley to the city.
passages.ot:
Jesus weeps as the prophets wept. Jeremiah cried out, “Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people” (Jeremiah 9:1). The Psalms had told Israel to “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem” (Psalm 122:6).

The words about the siege echo the prophets' warnings before the Babylonian army took the city in the 500s BC. Through Isaiah God said, “I will camp in a circle around you; I will besiege you with towers and set up siege works against you” (Isaiah 29:3).
passages.hard:
Is this God's verdict on the Jewish people? No. This is grief, not a verdict. The lament is not a sentence passed on the Jewish people. It was spoken by a Jew who loved Jerusalem, who longed to shelter it, and who wept over it. Christians have sometimes read this passage as if Jesus were announcing God's rejection of the Jews, and that reading fed contempt. It is wrong, and the site rejects it. Jesus speaks inside Israel, in the line of Jeremiah. His followers who sing in verse 38 are Jews. And a few verses later Luke says that “all the people hung on His words” (verse 48). The warning falls on any people, and any church, that does not know the hour when God comes near.

Were these words written after the city fell? Most scholars date Luke after AD 70, and many think these verses read like someone who knew how the siege went (see the book page). Others answer that the words fit any ancient siege, and echo the prophets' account of the Babylonian siege long before, so they need no hindsight. Careful readers hold each view. Either way, a prophet saying the city would fall was not new in Israel. What the passage stresses is not the accuracy of the forecast but its cause, and its tone, which is tears.
passages.asks: Jesus wept over the people who would reject him, before anything had happened. Ask whether you can grieve over a person or a place that has turned from God, instead of only being angry. If you are grieving someone who has walked away, he wept too. And ask whether God may be coming near to you today, in ways you have not stopped to notice.

passages.t: A house of prayer, and teaching every day
passages.happening:
Jesus goes into the temple courts and begins to drive out those who are selling there. He says, “It is written: ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” (verse 46).

From then on he teaches in the temple every day. The chief priests, the scribes and the leaders of the people want to kill him, but they cannot find a way, “because all the people hung on His words” (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene at length, and the note on Mark 11:15-19 explains the market in the temple's outer court, the money changers and the doves sold to the poor. Luke tells it in two verses. He wants the reader to see what happens next: Jesus takes over the temple as his classroom.

These last verses open a frame that runs to the end of chapter 21: “Every day Jesus taught at the temple” (21:37), and “early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple” (21:38). Inside that frame, the people listen and the leaders plot. Luke draws a clear line between the leaders who want Jesus dead and the ordinary Jewish people who hang on his words.

Jesus calls the temple ‘My house’. In Isaiah those are God's own words. And Luke, who began his book with a priest in the temple (1:8-9), now shows Jesus teaching there. The book will end there too (24:53).
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two prophets. Isaiah promised that God would bring foreigners to his temple, “for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7). Jeremiah warned those who felt safe because the temple stood: “Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?” (Jeremiah 7:11). A den is where robbers hide after their crimes.

Mark keeps Isaiah's words ‘for all the nations’. Matthew and Luke both leave them out. Some think Luke did so because, when he wrote, the temple had fallen and could no longer become that house. Others think he simply shortened the quotation, as he often does, and tells of the nations coming to God in his second book, Acts.

Malachi had promised that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1).
passages.hard:
What was Jesus doing? Christians and scholars read the scene in a few ways. Some see a cleansing: Jesus protests against greed and unfair trade in God's house and calls it back to prayer. Some see a sign of judgment: like Jeremiah, Jesus acts out the end of the temple, and in Luke he has just wept over its coming fall. These readings can overlap, and many hold more than one.

This was not Jesus attacking his own people's faith. He was a Jew speaking inside Israel's own tradition, as Jeremiah had, about the house of his Father. And Luke says that all the people hung on his words.
passages.asks: Jesus cleared space so that the temple could be what it was for, and then he filled it with teaching. Ask what has crowded out prayer in your own life, or in your church. Busy things are not always bad things. But a house of prayer needs room to pray.
